question: What is the difference between `reserve()` and `resize()`?

scenes.sub: One reserves memory. The other creates elements.
scenes.say: Reserve versus resize. They sound alike, and mixing them up is one of the most common vector bugs.

scenes.head: Same number, very different result
scenes.say: Reserve four only allocates. a has room for four ints, but its size is still zero. No elements exist. Resize four actually creates four elements, value initialized to zero, so b has size four. Now push back seven on both. a gets seven at index zero, exactly as you'd expect. b gets seven after the zeros, at index four, usually reallocating along the way. That's the classic bug: calling resize when you meant reserve, then pushing back, and ending up with twice as many elements.

scenes.head: Indexing, filling, shrinking
scenes.say: Second trap: indexing after reserve. v of zero is undefined behavior, because no element exists yet, even though the memory does. After resize, indexing is fine. Resize also takes a fill value, and it can shrink: elements past the new size are destroyed, but the capacity stays. Reserve never shrinks. Asking for less than the current capacity does nothing.

scenes.head: Side by side
rows: Yes: value-initialized, or copies of a fill value
You want n elements to index now
scenes.say: Size: reserve leaves it alone, resize sets it to n. Capacity: reserve raises it to at least n, resize grows it only if needed. Elements: only resize creates them. Shrinking: reserve never shrinks, resize can shrink the size, but not the capacity. So use reserve before a loop of push backs, and resize when you want n elements you can index right away.

lines: reserve(n): allocates memory only. Size unchanged, no elements created.
resize(n): changes the size, creating (or destroying) elements.
reserve + push_back, or resize + index. Never resize + push_back by accident.
scenes.say: Reserve allocates memory, but creates no elements. Resize changes the size, creating or destroying elements. Pair reserve with push back, and resize with indexing.
